doc.title: Hal Smith interviewed by Monk Rowe, Chautauqua, New York, September 12, 1997

title: Arbors sessions, studio time and overdubbing
summary: Listening to a Rick Fay Arbors session, Mat Domber's relaxed approach, rehearsal and overdubs.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Making records: studios, takes and the technology

blocks.x: Does this sound familiar to you?
That’s my splash cymbal. I only know a couple of other guys who would play it like that. That’s a Rick Fay session for Arbors.
Now on a session like this, I would imagine budget-wise you’re fairly tight with the studio time?
That one wasn’t. Actually Arbors doesn’t do that to musicians. Mat Domber is very loose about studio time and he doesn’t want the music to be forced. And he’s very fair in that respect.
So you get in there and do a run through and then—

You can do a run through and a couple of takes. I mean I don’t think any producer would want you to do the rehearsal in the studio and then do multiple takes. I mean you have an idea of what you’re going to do before you go in, but if it’s a specially assembled band that’s never seen the music, unless everybody’s an ace sight reader, you’re going to need some rehearsal time.
And there’s never, with this kind of music there’s never overdubbing.
Oh, no kidding. So they isolate people in the studio?

Not so much, no. What we’ve done a lot on sessions I’ve been involved in is if there’s a vocal for instance, where you don’t want to sing it live, you lay down the accompaniment beforehand. I mean say it’s Rebecca, anyone that I would have on a recording session would know how she sings and her phrasing. Like Chris Tyle, the trumpet player. He’d lay down the accompaniment and then she can come in later with the headphones and lay down the track.

You don’t like to do that, but there’s times with brass or something it might be too loud for her to hear herself, and the iso booth doesn’t — I hate that. If you can’t have everybody grouped together in the studio like you would play on a bandstand, that’s trouble just waiting to happen, because you can’t make the eye contact or little hand signals or something, that might save a performance otherwise. But there is a fair amount of overdubbing and clipping on of endings, and now you can do it with a computer, just match up the sound waves of the cymbal crash and no one will ever know. I’ll know but they won’t.
